AFTER-ACQUIRED EVIDENCE OF APPLICANT MISREPRESENTATION (MCKENNON; COOPER V. RYKOFF-SEXTON; CAMP V. JEFFER, MANGELS; MURILLO; SALAS V. SIERRA CHEMICAL; HORNE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about the "after-acquired evidence" doctrine as it applies to hiring: the situation in which an employer, after refusing to hire or discharging a person, discovers for the first time that the person misrepresented or concealed something on a job application or resume — a prior conviction, a falsified work history, work-authorization documents that were not genuine — or was otherwise ineligible for the job under a legal requirement the employer did not know had been violated. It draws on the United States Supreme Court's decision in McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co. (1995) 513 U.S. 352, which rejected after-acquired evidence as a complete bar to a federal age-discrimination claim while holding that it limits the remedies available; on three Court of Appeal decisions applying the doctrine to application misrepresentations — Cooper v. Rykoff-Sexton, Inc. (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 614 (no blanket rule that application falsification is a complete defense), Camp v. Jeffer, Mangels, Butler & Marmaro (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 620 (claims barred where the applicants concealed felony convictions that made them ineligible under a government-imposed job requirement), and Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc. (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 833 (employer must prove it would actually have refused to hire or would have discharged; claims arising during the employment are not barred); on the California Supreme Court's decision in Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co. (2014) 59 Cal.4th 407, which holds that neither after-acquired evidence nor unclean hands is a complete defense to a claim under the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), although both affect the remedies; and on Horne v. District Council 16 (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 524, which applied Salas to a refusal to hire. Where a specific employer and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. The sheet describes the doctrine as the courts have stated it; it does not address whether any particular statement on an application was false or material, and it does not restate the separate rules — covered in other information sheets in this corpus — that limit what an employer may ask an applicant about criminal history (the Fair Chance Act and Labor Code section 432.7) or that make labor-law protections available regardless of immigration status (Labor Code section 1171.5).

WHAT THE AFTER-ACQUIRED EVIDENCE DOCTRINE IS
The California Supreme Court has defined the doctrine this way: "The doctrine of after-acquired evidence refers to an employer’s discovery, after an allegedly wrongful termination of employment or refusal to hire, of information that would have justified a lawful termination or refusal to hire." (Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.) The definition reaches hiring decisions as well as discharges. The Court of Appeal in Camp v. Jeffer, Mangels, Butler & Marmaro described the doctrine's effect as one that "shields an employer from liability or limits available relief where, after a termination, the employer learns for the first time about employee wrongdoing that would have led to the discharge in any event," and observed that the wrongdoing at issue in such cases generally falls into one of two categories: "(1) misrepresentations on a resume or job application; or (2) posthire, on-the-job misconduct." This sheet concerns the first category. Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc. described the doctrine as one that "serves as a complete or partial defense to an employee’s claim of wrongful discharge" and that "comes into play when, after an employee’s termination, the employer learns of employee wrongdoing that would have resulted in the employee’s discharge in any event." Whether the defense is complete or partial, and what the employer must prove to invoke it, are the questions the decisions summarized in the following clauses answer. Two features of the doctrine follow from the definition. First, as Salas put it, "By definition, after-acquired evidence is not known to the employer at the time of the allegedly unlawful termination or refusal to hire"; the doctrine is therefore distinct from a mixed-motive case, in which the employer acted on both a lawful and an unlawful reason at the time of the decision. Second, the doctrine concerns information that would have justified the decision — it is about what the employer would have done had it known, which is why the decisions below turn on whether the employer can prove that it would in fact have refused to hire or would have discharged the person on the basis of what it later learned.

THE FEDERAL RULE: AFTER-ACQUIRED EVIDENCE LIMITS REMEDIES BUT DOES NOT BAR LIABILITY (MCKENNON V. NASHVILLE BANNER PUBLISHING CO.)
The modern framework comes from the United States Supreme Court's 1995 decision in McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., a case under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act in which the employer learned during the employee's deposition that she had copied confidential financial documents during her last year of employment. Assuming for purposes of summary judgment that the discharge was age-based and that the misconduct was grave enough that immediate discharge would have followed its disclosure, the Court rejected the lower courts' conclusion that after-acquired evidence of such wrongdoing "bars employees from any relief under the ADEA," calling that ruling "incorrect," and stated that it "would not accord with this scheme if after-acquired evidence of wrongdoing that would have resulted in termination operates, in every instance, to bar all relief for an earlier violation of the Act." The Court then held that the employee's wrongdoing nonetheless bears on the remedy: "The employee’s wrongdoing must be taken into account, we conclude, lest the employer’s legitimate concerns be ignored," not to punish the employee "but to take due account of the lawful prerogatives of the employer in the usual course of its business and the corresponding equities that it has arising from the employee’s wrongdoing." As a general rule in such cases, the Court concluded, "neither reinstatement nor front pay is an appropriate remedy. It would be both inequitable and pointless to order the reinstatement of someone the employer would have terminated, and will terminate, in any event and upon lawful grounds." For backpay, the Court stated that once an employer learns of wrongdoing that would lead to a legitimate discharge it cannot be required to ignore the information, "even if it is acquired during the course of discovery in a suit against the employer and even if the information might have gone undiscovered absent the suit," and that "[t]he beginning point in the trial court’s formulation of a remedy should be calculation of backpay from the date of the unlawful discharge to the date the new information was discovered." The Court also placed a threshold burden on the employer: where an employer seeks to rely on after-acquired evidence of wrongdoing, "it must first establish that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would" have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it at the time of the discharge. Finally, the Court acknowledged the concern that employers might routinely undertake extensive discovery into an employee's background to resist claims, calling it "not an insubstantial one," and stated that the courts' authority to award attorney's fees and to invoke the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure "will deter most abuses." McKennon involved on-the-job misconduct rather than an application misrepresentation, and a federal statute rather than California law; its significance for this sheet is that every California decision after 1995 summarized below builds on it.

NO BLANKET RULE THAT APPLICATION FALSIFICATION IS A COMPLETE DEFENSE (COOPER V. RYKOFF-SEXTON, INC.)
Cooper v. Rykoff-Sexton, Inc., decided by the Court of Appeal in 1994, a year before McKennon, was the first California decision to address application misrepresentations discovered after discharge. The court framed the question as "whether, as a matter of law, plaintiff’s claims are barred by material omissions in his employment application," omissions the employer "discovered… during the litigation." The employee, a commercial dishwashing-machine repairer, had worked for the employer for ten years without discipline before being fired over a half hour of overtime he recorded after skipping lunch; at his deposition the employer learned that his ten-year-old application had concealed that two prior employers had fired him and had misstated his work history. The employer's general manager declared, "If I had known about the omissions and misrepresentations in Cooper’s employment application, I would not have hired Mr. Cooper," and that the employee would have been discharged had the misrepresentations come to light during his employment. The court noted that a number of federal courts, "mostly overlooking the distinction between on-the-job misconduct and resumé falsification," had treated application fraud as defeating discrimination claims outright, and that "[m]any of those decisions probably reached the correct result on their facts." It nonetheless stated: "We decline to adopt a blanket rule that material falsification of an employment application is a complete defense to a claim that the employer, while still unaware of the falsification, terminated the employment in violation of the employee’s legal rights. Our reason is grounded in the facts of the case." Finding no California decisions in point, the court reasoned that "[n]either sound public policy nor the general law of contract dictates that an employee who can show that despite loyal and competent service he was fired without cause, in violation of a term of his employment contract—or because of his age, in violation of statute—nonetheless has forfeited all resulting legal remedies against his employer because of material misrepresentations he made years earlier in his employment application," that "[a]utomatic forfeiture of all employment rights regardless of the circumstances can be too harsh a penalty in many cases," and that where an employer fires a worker in violation of a statutory ban on discrimination the purpose of the antidiscrimination statutes would be "unacceptably undermined by a principle that would allow a fact that played no part in the firing decision to bar any recovery." The summary judgment was reversed. The court expressly left the effect of application fraud on damages undecided, noting in a footnote that the federal courts "have devoted Herculean labors to the task of ascertaining the effect of resumé fraud on damages" and that "[t]hat issue is not before us on this appeal."

A COMPLETE BAR WHERE THE MISREPRESENTED QUALIFICATION WAS IMPOSED BY LAW (CAMP V. JEFFER, MANGELS, BUTLER & MARMARO)
Camp v. Jeffer, Mangels, Butler & Marmaro, decided in 1995 after McKennon, is the California decision in which after-acquired evidence of an application misrepresentation operated as a complete bar. Two legal secretaries, a married couple, had each pleaded guilty in federal court to a felony involving false statements to a federally insured bank and had served prison time. When they applied to a law firm, "[t]he Camps each completed a job application that asked, among other things, if they had ever been convicted of a felony. They answered “no” to that question," and their resumes omitted the convictions and incarceration. The firm was a contractor for the Resolution Trust Corporation, and "[a]s a condition of representing the RTC, Jeffer Mangels was required to certify periodically that none of its employees had ever been convicted of a felony." The secretaries were later discharged and sued for wrongful termination; "[i]t was also during the litigation that Jeffer Mangels first learned that the Camps had been convicted of a felony." The Court of Appeal held that the couple's express at-will acknowledgments barred their contract and misrepresentation claims and that "the after-acquired-evidence doctrine bars their public policy claims." The court distinguished Cooper and McKennon on the ground that the job requirements in those cases were the employer's own: "While the job requirements and employer policies in all of those cases may have served legitimate business goals, the fact remains that they were self-imposed. Here, in contrast, the Camps misrepresented a job qualification imposed by the federal government, such that they were not lawfully qualified for the job." The misrepresentations, the court said, "went to the heart of their employment relationship with Jeffer Mangels," exposing the firm to loss of its RTC contract and to accusations of false certification. The court also recorded that the evidence established without contradiction that the couple would not have been hired had the firm known of the convictions and would have been terminated immediately had it learned of them during the employment, and it quoted McKennon's requirement that an employer relying on after-acquired evidence "must first establish that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it at the time of the discharge." Its holding was stated in these terms: "However, the equities compel a different result where an employee who is disqualified from employment by government-imposed requirements nevertheless obtains a job by misrepresenting the pertinent qualifications. In such a situation, the employee should have no recourse for an alleged wrongful termination of employment." Applying the doctrine of unclean hands, which "may apply to legal as well as equitable claims" in California, the court concluded: "Since the Camps were not lawfully qualified for their jobs, they cannot be heard to complain that they improperly lost them." The judgment for the employer was affirmed.

WHAT THE EMPLOYER MUST PROVE, AND CLAIMS THAT ARISE DURING THE EMPLOYMENT (MURILLO V. RITE STUFF FOODS, INC.)
Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc., decided in 1998 by the same division that decided Camp, addressed two questions Camp left open: what an employer must show to invoke the doctrine, and whether it reaches claims for injuries suffered during the employment rather than from the discharge. The plaintiff, an assembler, had purchased false resident alien and Social Security cards and "used these documents to secure her employment"; she sued for sexual harassment by her supervisor and related torts, and when the employer learned of the false documents at her deposition it moved for summary judgment on after-acquired evidence, supported by its president's declaration that it would not have hired her and would have fired her immediately. The court accepted that her misrepresentation "went to the heart of the employment relationship and related directly to her wrongful discharge and contractual claims" and that "[t]he unclean hands doctrine therefore would bar those claims" (which she had dismissed). But it held the after-acquired-evidence defense itself unproven. Quoting a federal decision, the court stated that the employer "must establish ‘that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it,’" and "must show that such a firing would have taken place as a matter of ‘settled’ company policy." The California Supreme Court has defined the doctrine this way: "The doctrine of after-acquired evidence refers to an employer’s discovery, after an allegedly wrongful termination of employment or refusal to hire, of information that would have justified a lawful termination or refusal to hire." (Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.) The definition reaches hiring decisions as well as discharges. The Court of Appeal in Camp v. Jeffer, Mangels, Butler & Marmaro described the doctrine's effect as one that "shields an employer from liability or limits available relief where, after a termination, the employer learns for the first time about employee wrongdoing that would have led to the discharge in any event," and observed that the wrongdoing at issue in such cases generally falls into one of two categories: "(1) misrepresentations on a resume or job application; or (2) posthire, on-the-job misconduct." Two features of the doctrine follow from the definition. First, as Salas put it, "By definition, after-acquired evidence is not known to the employer at the time of the allegedly unlawful termination or refusal to hire"; the doctrine is therefore distinct from a mixed-motive case, in which the employer acted on both a lawful and an unlawful reason at the time of the decision. Second, the doctrine concerns information that would have justified the decision — it is about what the employer would have done had it known, which is why the decisions below turn on whether the employer can prove that it would in fact have refused to hire or would have discharged the person on the basis of what it later learned.

expectedJSON.body: The modern framework comes from the United States Supreme Court's 1995 decision in McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., a case under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act in which the employer learned during the employee's deposition that she had copied confidential financial documents during her last year of employment. Assuming for purposes of summary judgment that the discharge was age-based and that the misconduct was grave enough that immediate discharge would have followed its disclosure, the Court rejected the lower courts' conclusion that after-acquired evidence of such wrongdoing "bars employees from any relief under the ADEA," calling that ruling "incorrect," and stated that it "would not accord with this scheme if after-acquired evidence of wrongdoing that would have resulted in termination operates, in every instance, to bar all relief for an earlier violation of the Act." The Court then held that the employee's wrongdoing nonetheless bears on the remedy: "The employee’s wrongdoing must be taken into account, we conclude, lest the employer’s legitimate concerns be ignored," not to punish the employee "but to take due account of the lawful prerogatives of the employer in the usual course of its business and the corresponding equities that it has arising from the employee’s wrongdoing." As a general rule in such cases, the Court concluded, "neither reinstatement nor front pay is an appropriate remedy. It would be both inequitable and pointless to order the reinstatement of someone the employer would have terminated, and will terminate, in any event and upon lawful grounds." For backpay, the Court stated that once an employer learns of wrongdoing that would lead to a legitimate discharge it cannot be required to ignore the information, "even if it is acquired during the course of discovery in a suit against the employer and even if the information might have gone undiscovered absent the suit," and that "[t]he beginning point in the trial court’s formulation of a remedy should be calculation of backpay from the date of the unlawful discharge to the date the new information was discovered." The Court also placed a threshold burden on the employer: where an employer seeks to rely on after-acquired evidence of wrongdoing, "it must first establish that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would" have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it at the time of the discharge. Finally, the Court acknowledged the concern that employers might routinely undertake extensive discovery into an employee's background to resist claims, calling it "not an insubstantial one," and stated that the courts' authority to award attorney's fees and to invoke the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure "will deter most abuses." McKennon involved on-the-job misconduct rather than an application misrepresentation, and a federal statute rather than California law; its significance for this sheet is that every California decision after 1995 summarized below builds on it.

expectedJSON.body: Cooper v. Rykoff-Sexton, Inc., decided by the Court of Appeal in 1994, a year before McKennon, was the first California decision to address application misrepresentations discovered after discharge. The court framed the question as "whether, as a matter of law, plaintiff’s claims are barred by material omissions in his employment application," omissions the employer "discovered… during the litigation." The employee, a commercial dishwashing-machine repairer, had worked for the employer for ten years without discipline before being fired over a half hour of overtime he recorded after skipping lunch; at his deposition the employer learned that his ten-year-old application had concealed that two prior employers had fired him and had misstated his work history. The employer's general manager declared, "If I had known about the omissions and misrepresentations in Cooper’s employment application, I would not have hired Mr. Cooper," and that the employee would have been discharged had the misrepresentations come to light during his employment. The court noted that a number of federal courts, "mostly overlooking the distinction between on-the-job misconduct and resumé falsification," had treated application fraud as defeating discrimination claims outright, and that "[m]any of those decisions probably reached the correct result on their facts." It nonetheless stated: "We decline to adopt a blanket rule that material falsification of an employment application is a complete defense to a claim that the employer, while still unaware of the falsification, terminated the employment in violation of the employee’s legal rights. Our reason is grounded in the facts of the case." Finding no California decisions in point, the court reasoned that "[n]either sound public policy nor the general law of contract dictates that an employee who can show that despite loyal and competent service he was fired without cause, in violation of a term of his employment contract—or because of his age, in violation of statute—nonetheless has forfeited all resulting legal remedies against his employer because of material misrepresentations he made years earlier in his employment application," that "[a]utomatic forfeiture of all employment rights regardless of the circumstances can be too harsh a penalty in many cases," and that where an employer fires a worker in violation of a statutory ban on discrimination the purpose of the antidiscrimination statutes would be "unacceptably undermined by a principle that would allow a fact that played no part in the firing decision to bar any recovery." The summary judgment was reversed. The court expressly left the effect of application fraud on damages undecided, noting in a footnote that the federal courts "have devoted Herculean labors to the task of ascertaining the effect of resumé fraud on damages" and that "[t]hat issue is not before us on this appeal."

expectedJSON.body: Camp v. Jeffer, Mangels, Butler & Marmaro, decided in 1995 after McKennon, is the California decision in which after-acquired evidence of an application misrepresentation operated as a complete bar. Two legal secretaries, a married couple, had each pleaded guilty in federal court to a felony involving false statements to a federally insured bank and had served prison time. When they applied to a law firm, "[t]he Camps each completed a job application that asked, among other things, if they had ever been convicted of a felony. They answered “no” to that question," and their resumes omitted the convictions and incarceration. The firm was a contractor for the Resolution Trust Corporation, and "[a]s a condition of representing the RTC, Jeffer Mangels was required to certify periodically that none of its employees had ever been convicted of a felony." The secretaries were later discharged and sued for wrongful termination; "[i]t was also during the litigation that Jeffer Mangels first learned that the Camps had been convicted of a felony." The Court of Appeal held that the couple's express at-will acknowledgments barred their contract and misrepresentation claims and that "the after-acquired-evidence doctrine bars their public policy claims." The court distinguished Cooper and McKennon on the ground that the job requirements in those cases were the employer's own: "While the job requirements and employer policies in all of those cases may have served legitimate business goals, the fact remains that they were self-imposed. Here, in contrast, the Camps misrepresented a job qualification imposed by the federal government, such that they were not lawfully qualified for the job." The misrepresentations, the court said, "went to the heart of their employment relationship with Jeffer Mangels," exposing the firm to loss of its RTC contract and to accusations of false certification. The court also recorded that the evidence established without contradiction that the couple would not have been hired had the firm known of the convictions and would have been terminated immediately had it learned of them during the employment, and it quoted McKennon's requirement that an employer relying on after-acquired evidence "must first establish that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it at the time of the discharge." Its holding was stated in these terms: "However, the equities compel a different result where an employee who is disqualified from employment by government-imposed requirements nevertheless obtains a job by misrepresenting the pertinent qualifications. In such a situation, the employee should have no recourse for an alleged wrongful termination of employment." Applying the doctrine of unclean hands, which "may apply to legal as well as equitable claims" in California, the court concluded: "Since the Camps were not lawfully qualified for their jobs, they cannot be heard to complain that they improperly lost them." The judgment for the employer was affirmed.

expectedJSON.body: Murillo v. Rite Stuff Foods, Inc., decided in 1998 by the same division that decided Camp, addressed two questions Camp left open: what an employer must show to invoke the doctrine, and whether it reaches claims for injuries suffered during the employment rather than from the discharge. The plaintiff, an assembler, had purchased false resident alien and Social Security cards and "used these documents to secure her employment"; she sued for sexual harassment by her supervisor and related torts, and when the employer learned of the false documents at her deposition it moved for summary judgment on after-acquired evidence, supported by its president's declaration that it would not have hired her and would have fired her immediately. The court accepted that her misrepresentation "went to the heart of the employment relationship and related directly to her wrongful discharge and contractual claims" and that "[t]he unclean hands doctrine therefore would bar those claims" (which she had dismissed). But it held the after-acquired-evidence defense itself unproven. Quoting a federal decision, the court stated that the employer "must establish ‘that the wrongdoing was of such severity that the employee in fact would have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it,’" and "must show that such a firing would have taken place as a matter of ‘settled’ company policy." Testimony that managers had been told most of the workforce was undocumented and had done nothing, and that the harassing supervisor himself had told the plaintiff where to buy false documents, was "enough to raise a question as to whether defendant actually would have refused to hire or fired plaintiff immediately upon learning of her undocumented status"; the employer therefore "failed to establish as a matter of law that, as a matter of settled company policy, it would have fired plaintiff immediately upon learning of her undocumented status." The court then held that, in any event, neither doctrine should bar her discrimination or tort claims, because, "[i]n contrast to the husband plaintiff in Camp, whose discrimination claim arose from his discharge, plaintiff’s discrimination and tort claims arise from acts occurring during her employment." It cautioned that "[c]ourts must tread carefully in applying the after-acquired-evidence doctrine to discrimination claims," stated that "while plaintiff was employed, she was entitled to all the protections available under employment law," and concluded: "Where, as here, the discriminatory conduct was pervasive during the term of employment, therefore, it would not be sound public policy to bar recovery for injuries suffered while employed. In applying the after-acquired-evidence doctrine, the equities between employer and employee can be balanced by barring all portions of the employment discrimination claim tied to the employee’s discharge." As to the tort claims, "no sort of “resumé fraud” could justify an employer’s discriminatory abuse of an employee." The summary judgment was reversed.

expectedJSON.body: The California Supreme Court settled the doctrine's application to FEHA claims in Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co. (2014). A seasonal production worker who had been injured on the job sued under FEHA for failure to accommodate and for retaliation after the employer did not rehire him. During the litigation the employer learned that the Social Security number he had used to obtain employment belonged to someone else, and it "sought a determination by the trial court that defendant was entitled to a judgment as a matter of law under the legal doctrines of after-acquired evidence and unclean hands, based on plaintiff’s fraudulent use of another person’s Social Security number and card to obtain employment with defendant." The Court of Appeal had held both doctrines complete defenses. The Supreme Court reversed, summarizing its holding as follows: "the doctrines of after-acquired evidence and unclean hands are not complete defenses to a worker’s claims under California’s FEHA, although they do affect the availability of remedies." It noted that the Court of Appeal had "read Camp and Murillo broadly as creating a complete defense based on after-acquired evidence" and had treated the Legislature as adopting that view in 2002, and stated, "We are not persuaded by the Court of Appeal’s reasoning on this point." On the merits it held that "[t]he high court’s reasoning in McKennon applies with equal force to plaintiff employee’s claim here that the employer violated plaintiff’s rights under California’s FEHA," and that "[t]o allow such after-acquired evidence to be a complete defense would eviscerate the public policies embodied in the FEHA by allowing an employer to engage in invidious employment discrimination with total impunity." But "[i]t does not follow, however, that the doctrine of after-acquired evidence has no bearing on employment discrimination and retaliation claims brought under California’s FEHA." The court described the general remedial rule in terms that expressly include applicants: "Generally, the employee’s remedies should not afford compensation for loss of employment during the period after the employer’s discovery of the evidence relating to the employee’s wrongdoing." And: "The remedial relief generally should compensate the employee for loss of employment from the date of wrongful discharge or refusal to hire to the date on which the employer acquired information of the employee’s wrongdoing or ineligibility for employment." The court explained that fashioning remedies on the relative equities "prevents the employer from violating California’s FEHA with impunity while also preventing an employee or job applicant from obtaining lost wages compensation for a period during which the employee or applicant would not in any event have been employed by the employer," and that "[i]n an appropriate case, it would also prevent an employee from recovering any lost wages when the employee’s wrongdoing is particularly egregious." The court also held, consistent with Murillo, that evidence the employer had looked the other way matters: testimony that a manager had assured workers with mismatched Social Security numbers that they would not be terminated "would support a finding that defendant employer deliberately chose to look the other way when put on notice of employees’ unauthorized status. Such a finding could affect application of the after-acquired evidence doctrine and thus the remedies available to plaintiff employee." On unclean hands, the court acknowledged that where the required showing is made the doctrine "may be a complete defense to legal as well as equitable causes of action," but held that "[e]quitable defenses such as unclean hands may not, however, be used to wholly defeat a claim based on a public policy expressed by the Legislature in a statute," that "equitable considerations may guide the court in fashioning relief in cases involving a legislatively expressed public policy," and that the Court of Appeal "erred in treating the doctrine of unclean hands as a complete defense to plaintiff’s lawsuit, an action founded upon public policies established by the Legislature in the FEHA."

expectedJSON.body: Horne v. District Council 16 International Union of Painters & Allied Trades (2015) applied Salas to a hiring decision. The plaintiff, a union member and local officer, twice applied for a union organizer position: "In 2009, Horne applied for an organizer position with District Council 16, without success. The man chosen to fill the position was White. In February 2010, Horne again applied for an organizer position with District Council 16. He was not hired, and the position was again filled by a White male." He sued under FEHA for race discrimination. During discovery he admitted a 1997 narcotics conviction, which the union contended disqualified him from the organizer position under a federal statute (29 U.S.C. § 504(a)). The court recorded that "[a]t the time of its February 2010 failure to hire Horne, District Council 16 did not know about Horne’s prior narcotics conviction: Neither it nor Local 718 had ever asked Horne if he had previously been convicted of a felony, and Horne had never volunteered the information" — so this was after-acquired evidence of ineligibility rather than of a false statement. The union "moved for summary judgment, arguing that undisputed facts established Horne’s inability to lawfully occupy the organizer position he sought in 2010 and that this circumstance was fatal to his discrimination claim," and the trial court agreed, holding that he could not show he was qualified and so could not state a prima facie case. The Court of Appeal, on remand from the Supreme Court for reconsideration in light of Salas, reversed. It stated that the dispute over using after-acquired evidence to negate the prima facie case "was essentially put to rest in June 2014, when the California Supreme Court issued its opinion in Salas," and that "Salas unambiguously states that after-acquired evidence cannot be used to completely bar a worker’s FEHA claims. Allowing such evidence to vitiate a plaintiff’s prima facie case would do precisely that." In the court's reading, "the clear import of Salas is that after-acquired evidence is simply irrelevant during all phases of the three-stage burden-shifting approach designed to establish liability." The court rejected the union's effort to confine Salas to undocumented workers: "We doubt that the state’s strong interest in providing employment conditions free of invidious discrimination applies any less to citizens previously convicted of crimes" than to undocumented workers. The union's factual arguments about the plaintiff's disqualification, the court said, "would be more appropriately addressed — should a conclusive determination ever be reached as to liability — during the trial court’s balancing of the equities for purposes of fashioning appropriate remedies." The court added that any award of pre-discovery lost wages "would be subject to a balancing of the equities based on the existence of the after-acquired evidence in this matter, and could, under appropriate circumstances, be limited or completely disallowed."

expectedJSON.body: Several other information sheets in this corpus describe rules that bear on the same facts. The sheets on the California Fair Chance Act (Government Code section 12952) and on Labor Code section 432.7 describe the limits on when an employer may ask an applicant about conviction history and what it may consider; the decisions summarized here (Camp, Horne) involved conviction histories, and Camp's application question predates those limits. The sheet on labor rights regardless of immigration status (Labor Code section 1171.5) describes the statute enacted in 2002 and the portion of Salas addressing federal preemption of lost-pay awards, which this sheet does not restate. The sheet on the mixed-motive "same-decision" defense (Harris v. City of Santa Monica) describes the different doctrine that applies when the employer acted on both a lawful and an unlawful reason at the time of its decision, as opposed to a reason it learned of only afterward. The sheets on background checks, the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, and background-check adverse-action notices describe the procedures that govern an employer's use of consumer reports to verify an applicant's statements before a decision is made. The sheet on fraudulent inducement of employment describes claims that run in the other direction — by an applicant against an employer for misrepresentations made to induce acceptance of a job. This sheet does not restate any of those materials.
